brief:
Review explanation

Choosing a Decision Tree Split: Move the Cutoff, Compare Gini and Entropy

interactive
How does a decision tree choose where to split? Let me move a cutoff through a few labeled points, switch between Gini and entropy, and reveal the best split so I can compare it with mine.

Presentation
Static
Steps
Over time
Experiment

You'll see about a dozen points in two colours (two classes) on a single number line, with a vertical cutoff line splitting them into a left group and a right group. As you move the cutoff, it shows how many of each colour fall on each side, the impurity of each side, their weighted average, and how much impurity the split removes compared with the unsplit set, with the formula shown. This shows that a tree picks the cutoff that leaves each side as close to one colour as possible, weighted by how many points end up on each side. Switching between Gini and entropy recalculates every number, so you can see whether the two measures agree on which cutoffs are good. Pressing the reveal button marks the best cutoff and draws the weighted impurity for every possible cutoff as a curve, so you can compare your choice with the lowest point on the curve.

ASSUMPTIONS 3
LIMITATIONS 3

findings.message: At the default cutoff x = 3.0 the learner's vertical cutoff line runs straight through the circle for the B point at x = 2.9 and over its letter. This obscures the point the split is about. A default away from any point, such as 2.5, would avoid it.
The panel prints raw underscores ('I_L', 'I_R') instead of subscripts. It doesn't match the typeset formula above it.
No capture uses the Entropy setting, so I could not check entropy values or that option from this sample.
The cutoff line at x = 3.0 runs through the circle for the B point at x = 2.9 and covers its letter.
The curve's horizontal scale (70+52x) differs from the number line's (60+54x). The curve's 'best' marker sits about 3 px left of the green best-cutoff line above it, so the two don't line up exactly.
After Reset, the cutoff line at x = 3.0 runs through the circle for the B point at x = 2.9 and covers its letter.
After Hide, the cutoff line at x = 3.0 runs through the circle for the B point at x = 2.9 and covers its letter.
After pressing Reveal four times, the cutoff line at x = 3.0 runs through the circle for the B point at x = 2.9 and covers its letter.
The Entropy measure and the lowest cutoff value were not sampled, so the entropy readouts could not be checked against captures. The source's log2 entropy code looks correct.
The n_L/n and n_R/n fractions in the weighted-impurity formula are rendered very small. They are readable but could be larger.

manifest.title: Choosing a decision tree split: Gini vs entropy
manifest.summary: Twelve points from two classes sit on a number line. Move the cutoff to see the class counts on each side, each side's impurity, the size-weighted average and how much impurity the split removes. Switch between Gini and entropy, then reveal the best cutoff and the curve of weighted impurity for every cutoff.
assumptions: The points have one numeric feature and two classes (6 A, 6 B).
The best cutoff is searched among midpoints between neighbouring points, as in standard decision tree methods.
Entropy is measured in bits (log base 2).
The point set is fixed. Only one split on one feature is shown.
manifest.description: A number line from 0 to 10 holds 12 circles labelled A or B. A vertical line marks your cutoff. On the right, text lists the A and B counts and impurity for each side, the weighted impurity formula and its value, the impurity of the unsplit set and the impurity removed. After you press Reveal, a green line marks the best cutoff, and a step curve below shows weighted impurity against cutoff position, with your cutoff and the lowest point marked.

brief.title: Choosing a Decision Tree Split: Move the Cutoff, Compare Gini and Entropy
brief.summary: You'll see about a dozen points in two colours (two classes) on a single number line, with a vertical cutoff line splitting them into a left group and a right group. As you move the cutoff, it shows how many of each colour fall on each side, the impurity of each side, their weighted average, and how much impurity the split removes compared with the unsplit set, with the formula shown. This shows that a tree picks the cutoff that leaves each side as close to one colour as possible, weighted by how many points end up on each side. Pressing the reveal button marks the best cutoff and draws the weighted impurity for every possible cutoff as a curve, so you can compare your choice with the lowest point on the curve.
assumptions: The points have a single numeric feature and two classes.
Possible cutoffs sit halfway between neighbouring points, as in standard decision tree methods.
Entropy is measured in bits (log base 2).
limitations: It shows only one split on one feature, not choosing between several features or growing a full tree.
The labelled points are a fixed example set, so you can't add or move them.
Overfitting, stopping rules and pruning are not covered.
